page_title: Authorization Logic: Rules are hard because they evolve over time

sources.entry: Authorization Logic: Rules are hard because they evolve over time

summary.title: Authorization Logic: Rules are hard because they evolve over time
summary.one_liner: Authorization rules get hard because they start as a quick admin flag and then evolve through predictable maturity stages, and this post maps those stages to the three main classes of rule tooling.
takeaways: Authorization rules begin simply (e.g., an admin boolean) but grow in complexity as the product adds collaboration, attributes and resource-level roles.
A maturity model moves from application-wide access, to resource-specific access, to user-configurable permissions, to custom policies.
Three solution classes are compared: language-specific libraries (Pundit, CASL, Shiro), Zanzibar clones (OpenFGA), and DSLs (Oso, OPA).
Good authorization tooling should be easy to implement, opinionated, start simple, mix models (RBAC, ReBAC, ABAC) and support custom rules.
summary.summary: The post is Part 2 of a five-part series on why authorization is hard, focusing on rules. It argues that authorization logic is a rule set governing who can do what, and that simple early implementations (like an admin boolean) lead to repeated rewrites as requirements grow. It presents a maturity model running from application-wide roles through resource-specific access, user-configurable permissions, and custom policies. It then compares three classes of solutions (language-specific libraries, Zanzibar clones, and DSLs such as Oso and OPA) using examples like Pundit, OpenFGA, and Oso policies, and argues that opinionated defaults help teams avoid rewrites. Note: the page is written by Oso and promotes its product.
